purpose: This medication is used to treat certain types of cancer, including breast cancer, lung cancer, and pancreatic cancer. Your doctor has prescribed it to help stop cancer cells from growing and spreading in your body.
how_it_works: Think of cancer cells as cells that keep dividing and multiplying out of control. This medicine works by interfering with that process — it essentially 'freezes' the cancer cells so they can't divide anymore and eventually die off. It is attached to a protein called albumin, which helps carry the medicine directly to the cancer cells more effectively.
common_side_effects: You may experience hair loss, numbness or tingling in your hands and feet, nausea, vomiting, tiredness, muscle or joint pain, low blood cell counts (which can increase your risk of infection or bleeding), and diarrhea. Many of these side effects are manageable, so please let your care team know if anything feels bothersome.
warnings: This medicine can seriously lower your white blood cell count, making it easier for you to get infections — contact your doctor right away if you develop a fever. It can cause nerve damage (tingling, numbness, or pain in hands and feet). Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can harm your baby. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, as some can interact with this drug.
typical_dosing: This medication is given as an IV infusion (through a vein) by a nurse or doctor, usually in a clinic or hospital. The dose and how often you receive it depends on the type of cancer being treated — it may be given weekly or every 3 weeks. Your doctor will determine the right schedule for you based on your specific situation and how your body responds to treatment.
